reference.source: Standard nephrology and clinical genetics references
clinicalPearls: Driven by two renal-risk variants (G1 and G2) in APOL1 that are common in people of West African ancestry
A high-risk genotype means two risk alleles (any combination of G1 and G2); it substantially raises the risk of several kidney diseases
Associated phenotypes include focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, HIV-associated nephropathy, hypertension-attributed CKD, and more rapid CKD progression
Inheritance behaves recessively for kidney risk, but most people with two risk alleles never develop kidney disease, indicating that a 'second hit' is usually required
The variants persist at high frequency because a single copy confers protection against African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness)
Recognising APOL1 risk has implications for living kidney donation and for donor-derived graft outcomes
Genotyping identifies risk but does not by itself diagnose active kidney disease, which still needs clinical and, where appropriate, histological assessment
reference.pathophysiology: APOL1 encodes apolipoprotein L1, a circulating and intracellular protein that also confers innate immunity against certain trypanosomes. The G1 and G2 coding variants alter the protein so that, in the presence of a second environmental or genetic stressor (such as interferon-driven inflammation from viral infection), APOL1 becomes toxic to kidney cells, particularly podocytes. This injury drives podocyte dysfunction and loss, producing focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, collapsing glomerulopathy and progressive glomerular and interstitial scarring. Because injury generally requires a two-hit process, the high-risk genotype increases susceptibility and accelerates progression rather than being sufficient alone to cause disease.
additionalDifferentials: HIV-associated nephropathy without APOL1 risk genotype
Membranous nephropathy and other glomerular diseases
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis and urine protein-to-creatinine or albumin-to-creatinine ratio to quantify proteinuria
Serum creatinine with eGFR trajectory over time
Blood pressure assessment given the hypertension-linked phenotype
Kidney biopsy where the pattern of glomerular disease needs clarification
APOL1 genotyping (G1 and G2) in appropriate clinical and donor-evaluation contexts
Screening for secondary triggers such as HIV and other relevant viral infections
redFlags: Nephrotic-range proteinuria with rapidly declining renal function
Collapsing glomerulopathy on biopsy, often with an interferon-associated trigger
Accelerated CKD progression despite blood pressure control
Deteriorating graft function in a kidney from a high-risk-genotype donor
reference.prognosis: The high-risk genotype is linked to earlier onset and faster progression of kidney disease, but penetrance is incomplete and many carriers retain normal kidney function; outcome depends heavily on the presence of a second injurious trigger and on control of blood pressure and proteinuria.
pitfalls: Treating APOL1 genotype as diagnostic of disease rather than a susceptibility factor
Neglecting the impact of the genotype on living-donor evaluation and counselling
Assuming a Mendelian dominant pattern rather than the recessive-acting two-hit model
Overlooking a treatable second hit such as viral infection driving collapsing disease
references: KDIGO / peer-reviewed reviews on APOL1 kidney disease
management: Control blood pressure and proteinuria with renin-angiotensin system blockade using an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin-receptor blocker
Add an SGLT2 inhibitor for additional renoprotection in proteinuric chronic kidney disease
Identify and treat the second hit, including antiretroviral therapy for HIV-associated nephropathy and control of interferon-driven viral triggers
Use biopsy-guided corticosteroid immunosuppression where a treatable focal segmental or collapsing glomerulosclerosis lesion is demonstrated
Monitor eGFR trajectory and urine protein-to-creatinine ratio with regular blood-pressure surveillance for progression
Refer to nephrology and consider enrolment in trials of APOL1-targeted inhibitor therapy
Plan renal replacement therapy and transplant assessment as chronic kidney disease advances
Provide genetic counselling and APOL1 genotyping in living-donor evaluation and family assessment given West African ancestry and recessive kidney-risk inheritance
